source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers exploratory play (Exp 1)
finding: Preschoolers rarely isolated a candidate cause when the evidence was unambiguous, and did so about half the time when it was ambiguous. This is the human anchor for every machine study below.
numbers: N=60 (mean age about 54 months, range 46-64), 20 per condition. Informative intervention (pulling the separable bead pair apart): All Beads 1/20 (5%); Some Beads B 9/20 (45%); Some Beads AB 10/20 (50%). Chi-square(1,N=40)=8.53 and 10.16, both p<.005. Snapping the pair apart on the toy: 63% vs 18% (chi-square 9.37, p<.005).
limits: Small cells; one toy family; human only.
agent_relevance: This is the behaviour S7 and open-mode S3 want: spend tests only where evidence leaves hypotheses tied. No LLM study found reproduces this ambiguity gate directly (see c31).

source: Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers exploratory play (Exp 2)
finding: Given ambiguous evidence, children also designed the informative test themselves, without being shown it.
numbers: N=40 (45% girls), 20 per condition. Informative experiment: Some Beads 9/20 (45%) vs All Beads 1/20 (5%); chi-square(1,N=40)=8.53, p<.005. Coder agreement 86%, kappa .71.
limits: Same lab and toy family; no large independent replication located this session.
agent_relevance: Evidence that test selection can be gated by what the data leave open. A program can compute that gate (count of hypotheses still consistent) instead of asking the model to feel it.

source: Kosoy, Liu, Collins, Chan et al. (2022) Learning causal overhypotheses through exploration in children and computational models (CLeaR)
finding: Children aged 4-6 explored a blicket machine with or without being told the hypothesis space. Telling them made their exploration far more likely to settle the rule.
numbers: N per cell: not-given conjunctive 20, given conjunctive 22, not-given disjunctive 20, given disjunctive 23. Mean unique combinations 3.85, 5.36, 3.70, 5.43. Enough data to fully determine the truth: 71% given vs 32% not given (p=0.002, two-proportion z). Tested the empty machine: 17.7% / 17.5%. Tried different orderings: 66.7% / 65%.
limits: Online iPad sample; about 85 children over four cells; children did not use the given hypothesis space to skip pointless tests.
agent_relevance: Giving the model an explicit short list of live hypotheses (S2) probably matters more than asking it to be curious: unbounded hypothesis spaces gave unfocused exploration even in children.

source: Kosoy et al. (2022) CLeaR: children versus ideal-observer and minimum-step models
finding: Information-gain-optimal models take fewer steps than children and always collect enough data. Children took more steps, did not vary with rule type, and often stopped with the rule unsettled.
numbers: Children took more steps than agents in every condition. Given-disjunctive: children differ from minimum-step and per-step models at p<0.0001. Models always generated enough observations to disambiguate; children did so 71% (given) and 32% (not given).
limits: Optimal models assume a known hypothesis set. The authors favour 'children optimise for a wider set of alternatives' over 'noisy optimal'; not proven.
agent_relevance: An optimal-information-gain agent is a poor model of a child. Code-side information gain is still the right selector for us, but children are not proof it is natural.

source: Kosoy, Chan, Liu, Collins et al. (2022) Towards understanding how machines can learn causal overhypotheses (RL agents)
finding: Blicket-detector benchmark for RL agents. Decision transformers and behaviour cloning trained on policy data did poorly. Forced extra random exploration helped most.
numbers: Decision Transformer reward 0.16 (random data) vs 2.06, 2.16, 2.37 with 5, 10, 15 forced exploration steps; forced-choice accuracy (conjunctive vs disjunctive) 0.67 to 0.77. Behaviour cloning reward about -0.16 to 0.22 in every setting, accuracy 0.55 to 0.68. A2C/PPO-trained data rewards 0.14 to 0.74.
limits: Workshop paper; small reward scale.
agent_relevance: Forced exploration before commitment beat expert imitation. Maps to open-mode S3: force untried actions first, then select.

source: Kosoy et al. (2022) Towards understanding how machines can learn causal overhypotheses (GPT-3 and PaLM on blicket text)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-002, temp 0.7) and PaLM nearly always picked the right causal structure when given the hypotheses, but GPT-3 named too many objects as blickets, including ones tied to other machines. PaLM struggled when its examples did not cover the true hypothesis space.
numbers: Table 2 holds a handful of freeform items per condition (for example 'given hypotheses, disjunctive: 1/1 correct, 6 wrong'; 'not given, conjunctive: 2/2' and '0/1'). No percentages with a real N.
limits: Tiny item counts; 2022 models; text-only data.
agent_relevance: Anecdotal. The point that stays: the hypothesis list must be supplied or generated, because the model cannot be trusted to derive it.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023, PNAS) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (information search)
finding: GPT-3 used rudimentary random exploration but no directed exploration (it did not pick the more informative arm more often when the horizon was longer). It was biased toward options it had already seen more often.
numbers: Horizon x estimated-reward-difference interaction beta=-0.02, z=-1.47, p=.14 (not strategic). Horizon effect in the unequal-information condition beta=-0.15, z=-0.56, p=.58 (directed exploration absent; humans show it). Reward-difference effect beta=0.18, z=14.48, p<.001.
limits: GPT-3 (2022). Newer models differ (see c26).
agent_relevance: Early evidence that a plain model does not choose the informative test by itself. Choosing the informative test is a job for code.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (causal reasoning)
finding: GPT-3 passed a simple text blicket item, an intervention item and a pill-counterfactual item, but failed the harder test that separates observing from intervening in a causal chain.
numbers: Blicket vignette: correct (first object blicket, second not). Common-cause condition: matched normative do-operator inference. Causal-chain: predictions identical to common-cause (should differ); did not lower its prediction after observing B=0. Standard vignettes: 12 of 12 answered correctly or with human-like errors, six exactly correct.
limits: One model; the authors warn vignettes may be in the training data and that small rewording broke it.
agent_relevance: Passing a vignette is weak evidence of ability to run an informative test. Judge exploration from behaviour in a live loop, not vignettes (G10 in spirit).

source: Kosoy, Reagan, Lai, Gopnik, Cobb (2023) Comparing machines and children: developmental psychology experiments and LaMDA
finding: LaMDA did worst in the causal reasoning domain, which included the blicket induction and disjunctive/conjunctive blicket tasks. It could not track the evidence and fell back on the commonest causal story.
numbers: Average LRS by domain: Social and Moral 4.33; Perception 2.91; Theory of Mind 2.86; Causal Reasoning 1.34 (worst). LaMDA cited the researchers own blicket papers in answers, so the word was renamed 'Zerpda'.
limits: Rubric graded by the authors; one model; contamination by the published paradigm is a real risk.
agent_relevance: Contamination warning for any test of our agent on blicket-style items: use renamed or newly built machines.

source: Yiu, Kosoy, Gopnik (2023) Imitation versus innovation: what children can do that LLMs cannot (yet)
finding: Large language and vision-language models imitated associations well but were worse than children and adults at choosing an unusual but functionally right tool, and struggled to learn causal overhypotheses from interactive data.
numbers: Tool task: children n=42 (mean age 5.71) and adults n=30 recognised associated objects 88.4% and 84.9%; picked the unrelated functional object 85.2% and 95.7%. Models matched on association but chose the coffee lid over the plant pot to hold hot coffee. No new numbers for LLMs on blicket in this position paper.
limits: Position paper; LLM tool-task numbers are in figures, not text.
agent_relevance: Models give the statistically nearest answer. Open-mode S3 needs forced distance from the typical answer, as the schema says.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus, Marino (2025, COLM) Language agents mirror human causal reasoning biases
finding: On an interactive blicket test, language models identified disjunctive (OR) machines far better than conjunctive (AND) machines. The bias held across GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, QwQ and Gemma3, across default, ReAct, Reflexion and chain-of-thought prompts, and it grew with 8 objects versus 4.
numbers: At least 16 independent trials per model, prompt and system message; 4 or 8 objects, 2 blickets, 32-action limit. An information-gain oracle reaches Q&A accuracy 1.0 on both rules. Model accuracies appear only in figures (Fig 2, 11).
quote: systematically struggle with the unusual, yet equally (or sometimes even more) evidenced conjunctive ones
limits: Numbers only in plots; no new human data collected.
agent_relevance: Prompt styles (ReAct, Reflexion, CoT) did not remove the bias. Do not expect a thinking-style prompt to fix test selection (matches section 4b).

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Information gain predicts success; reasoning length and early exit predict failure
finding: The best predictor of final success was the information gathered by exploration. Models that stopped early did worse, and longer replies went with lower accuracy.
numbers: Spearman across model-prompt-rule combinations, 8-object setting (read from Fig 3): information gain rho about 0.76 (strongest); unique states visited about 0.33; steps before exit about -0.35; response length about -0.30 (p<0.05 for length).
limits: Correlational, read from a figure; points are model-prompt combinations, not independent trials.
agent_relevance: Supports ranking candidate tests by information gain in code (G5) and a short-answer bias (G11).

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Exploration efficiency of LM agents versus an oracle and random
finding: No language model eliminated hypotheses as fast as the information-gain oracle. GPT-4o was best of the models. Gemma3 and DeepSeek-R1 sometimes did worse than random actions.
numbers: Oracle reduces the hypothesis set to 1 in few steps; LM agents fall behind, especially for AND rules and 8 objects. No exact step counts in text.
limits: Plot-only evidence.
agent_relevance: Plain 'think then act' agents waste experiments. A program that proposes the discriminating action beats a model that chooses it.

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Does better data fix the bias? Same exploration data given to every model
finding: Giving models the oracle's exploration trace improved conjunctive accuracy, so poor exploration partly causes poor answers. But for all except DeepSeek-R1 accuracy stayed below perfect, and GPT-4o still did worse on AND than OR even with oracle data.
numbers: Data sources compared: GPT-4o's own exploration, oracle, random, count-based. All models improved on AND with oracle data; only deepseek-reasoner near perfect. Values in Fig 5 only.
limits: Exact values only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Two separate failures: choosing tests (fixable by code) and drawing conclusions from them (a prior that persists).

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Comparison with human adults and 4-year-olds
finding: Replicating Lucas et al. 2014 and Gopnik et al. 2017, models leaned toward 'disjunctive' on ambiguous data like adults, while 4-year-olds correctly inferred a conjunctive machine when the evidence supported it.
numbers: Human percentages come from Gopnik et al. 2017 and appear only in Fig 6; the text gives no counts.
limits: Adult-versus-child contrast is qualitative here.
agent_relevance: Models are adult-like: strong priors, less open to unusual structure than children. Argues for forcing low-prior hypotheses into the candidate set.

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Exploration breadth by rule: models versus children (Kosoy et al. 2022b data)
finding: Children explored about equally whether the rule was AND or OR (unbiased curiosity). LMs tried fewer unique combinations and stopped sooner in the disjunctive condition, so their exploration depends on their beliefs.
numbers: 3-object setting with system prompts matched to the psychology scripts; two-sample t-tests significant for LMs and not for children (Fig 7).
limits: Child numbers from CLeaR Table 1; small samples.
agent_relevance: Model effort tracks its own belief: it stops when it feels sure, which is the wrong gate. Use a code-side count of live hypotheses to decide when to stop.

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) Test-time hypothesis sampling and elimination
finding: The fix: sample many distinct hypotheses as Python functions, reject duplicates to build a flat prior, then tell the model to choose actions that eliminate as many as possible. More initial samples gave better exploration and removed the AND/OR gap.
numbers: 8-object environment, initial unique hypotheses 16, 32, 64, 96: Q&A accuracy rose with the count and, with enough samples, showed no drop for AND versus OR (Fig 9b, values in figure only). Also removed the disjunctively biased exploration pattern (App C.5.4).
limits: Needs a hypothesis space expressible as code; cost grows with samples; numbers read from a figure.
agent_relevance: Closest existing method to our S2 plus S7: enumerate hypotheses, then pick the test that cuts the list most. Strong candidate to adopt, with a code-run elimination check.

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik, Precup (2026, CogSci) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration?
finding: Adults handle conjunctive rules well once they choose their own tests; the old adult 'conjunctive handicap' came from passive evidence. LLMs did not consistently gain from choosing their own interventions and trailed top humans on AND rules.
numbers: 306 adults on Prolific (102 per condition: Active, Passive Observer, Passive Proposer). Mean tests to success, AND / OR: humans 9.6 / 6.4; top human 8.5 / 3.8; gpt-5 10.2 / 7.7; gpt-5-mini 10.8 / 7.1; gemini-2.5-flash 13.5 / 9.7; deepseek-reasoner 8.2 / 6.8; o4-mini 6.7 / 4.2; deepseek-chat 12.3 / 11.9. Average adult: 16% wrong on both rule and objects in AND.
limits: New novel-name 'nexiom' task; models drive a text game; prompt details not reproduced here.
agent_relevance: Newest direct human-versus-LLM comparison. Reasoning models (gpt-5, deepseek-reasoner) match top humans on OR; chat models lag far behind on AND.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Passive Proposer control: is the benefit planning or contingent feedback?
finding: People who planned tests but saw the results of someone else's tests did as badly as passive learners. The benefit of exploring comes from seeing the result of your own test and updating, not from planning tests.
numbers: Conjunctive object identification: Active Explorer 0.69; Passive Observer 0.45; Passive Proposer 0.12. Rule selection: 0.82, 0.69, 0.57.
limits: Human only; the authors do not test whether the same holds for agents.
agent_relevance: For an agent loop: run each test and feed the result straight back before choosing the next test (G2). Do not batch a plan of tests in one pass.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Model exploration style and time per test
finding: Stronger reasoning models showed a human-like move from one-object tests to targeted two-object tests as uncertainty fell. Weaker models stayed unfocused and used more tests.
numbers: Seconds per test AND / OR: gpt-5 44.3 / 43.0; deepseek-reasoner 65.2 / 58.2; gemini-2.5-flash 9.6 / 11.1; deepseek-chat 5.5 / 6.0; humans about 31.5 / 23.5. Fast chat models used the most tests (deepseek-chat 12.3 / 11.9).
limits: Latency, not tokens; confounded by API speed.
agent_relevance: Cheap fast models over-test; slow reasoning models test less and better. Consistent with 'think too fast' (c24).

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to falsify: confirmation bias in language models
finding: On a Wason 2-4-6 style rule discovery game, eleven LLMs mostly proposed confirming triples. Less confirmation (more incompatible tests) went with more success. A 'Think-in-Opposites' (TiO) prompt raised discovery from 42% to 56% on average.
numbers: Eleven LLMs; task success from 6% to 78% within 45 turns. LLaMA-3.3-70B non-thinking: baseline 0.21, TiO 0.38, Dual-Goal 0.20. Qwen3-32B non-thinking: baseline 0.33, TiO 0.36, Dual-Goal 0.10.
limits: Per-model table partly garbled in text extraction, so only unambiguous cells are quoted here. Dual-Goal needs an opposite hypothesis, which many tasks lack.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for S7: a prompt that asks for the test that would break the leading rule helps. A generic 'consider both sides' prompt (Dual-Goal) can hurt.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Think-in-Opposites on the Blicket test (192 episodes per model-prompt)
finding: On blicket (AND/OR/XOR, 4 or 8 objects, 2 or 3 blickets) TiO helped thinking models much more than non-thinking ones. Across both, success correlated with the share of incompatible tests.
numbers: Qwen3-32B thinking 0.57 to 0.86 (I:C 0.54 to 1.31). Qwen3-8B thinking 0.32 to 0.40. Qwen3-14B thinking 0.50 to 0.61. Qwen3-32B non-thinking fell 0.64 to 0.56. LLaMA-3.3-70B 0.78 to 0.82. Spearman correlation of I:C with success 0.65 (thinking) and 0.74 (non-thinking), read from Fig 4.
limits: Paired permutation tests in appendix; gains small for non-thinking models and can be negative.
agent_relevance: Use the opposite-test prompt only in reasoning mode, or where a check can confirm it helped (G7).

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Distilling falsification behaviour from Wason to Blicket
finding: Fine-tuning on falsification-style traces from the number game transferred to blicket, but gave less than a task-specific prompt.
numbers: Qwen3-8B base 0.32, TiO prompt 0.40, Wason-distilled 0.34. Qwen3-32B base 0.57 vs TiO prompt 0.86 (the distilled 32B student gained less).
limits: Training, not scaffolding; small effects at 8B.
agent_relevance: The skill is learnable but the cheap prompt-plus-code route is stronger for us.

source: Pan, Xie, Wilson (2025) Large language models think too fast to explore effectively (Little Alchemy 2)
finding: Open-ended element-combination game. Most LLMs found fewer new elements than humans; only o1 (and DeepSeek-R1) beat them. Regression shows models lean on uncertainty and ignore empowerment (future possibilities).
numbers: 500 trials per LLM; elements found: LLaMA3.1-8B 9; LLaMA3.1-70B 25; GPT-4o 35; DeepSeek-R1 85; o1 177; humans 42 within 500 trials and 51 across all trials (29,493 players, 4,691,033 trials). o1 t=9.71 p<0.001; R1 t=3.40 p<0.027; GPT-4o t=-5.48; LLaMA-70B t=-6.39; LLaMA-8B t=-28.12. Temperature x uncertainty beta=2.911 (z=7.44); temperature x empowerment beta=0.196 (p=0.286).
limits: One game; closed model internals unknown; DeepSeek-R1 tried more failed combinations than humans.
agent_relevance: Open-ended exploration scales with reasoning-trained models, not with temperature. Temperature is not the lever for diverse exploration, which supports a code-kept history of directions tried.

source: Pan, Xie, Wilson (2025) Sparse-autoencoder analysis: why LLMs decide too early
finding: In LLaMA3.1-70B, uncertainty and the choice are represented in early layers, but empowerment only in later layers, so the decision is made before empowerment can enter.
numbers: SAE correlation: uncertainty peaks at layer 2; choice beta peaks at layer 1; empowerment peaks at layer 72 (Fig 5). Reasoning models spend more tokens and revisit earlier combinations.
limits: Correlational interpretability on one open model; not tested causally.
agent_relevance: Supports a program that forces a gap between candidate generation and choice, and scores candidates on longer-run value in code.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024, NeurIPS) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: On multi-armed bandits, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 did not explore robustly. Only GPT-4 with chain of thought, a suggestive framing and an externally summarised history worked.
numbers: GPT-4 basic prompt had suffix failures (stops sampling the best arm) in more than 60% of replicates. 2^5 = 32 prompt designs per model, 72 GPT-4 configurations; one succeeded (BSSC0). About 200K queries for GPT-3.5 and Llama2, about 50K for GPT-4.
limits: Bandits, not causal tasks; 2023 models; the summarised history is a manual aid.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as c07: code should summarise history as sufficient statistics rather than letting the model reread a long log.

source: Gandhi, Li, Goodyear, Bhatia, Li, Bhaskar, Zaman, Goodman (2025) BoxingGym: automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: Ten generative-model environments scored by expected information gain (EIG) of the experiments chosen. All tested LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen-2.5, OpenThinker) struggled at both experimental design and model discovery.
numbers: EIG regret and standardised prediction error per environment. GPT-4o had the lowest EIG regret and good prediction; Qwen-32B had higher EIG regret with good prediction. Adding explicit statistical models (Box's Apprentice) did not beat plain GPT-4o consistently. Predictions after 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 10 experiments.
limits: Exact table values are in the appendix; hyperbolic discounting stayed hard even after experiments.
agent_relevance: A ready benchmark with an EIG metric we could use to test an S7 discriminating test. Good predictors can still choose poor experiments.

source: Jansen, Cote, Khot et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: virtual environment for automated scientific discovery agents
finding: 120 text-world discovery tasks across 8 topics. Baseline agents (including ReAct and a Hypothesizer agent) did poorly compared with human scientists.
numbers: Humans: 66% average task completion, 55% explanatory knowledge. Best agent ReAct completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks. Hypothesizer found 34% of gold knowledge on easy and 8% on challenge.
limits: Baselines are GPT-4o era; only best-agent figures read.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis-first agents found more explanation but finished fewer tasks; a test-selection layer would need both.

source: Alderete, Benthall, Xu, Xing (2026) Separable pathways for causal reasoning: architectural scaffolding for hypothesis-space restructuring
finding: A scaffold with a typed exploration state machine (context graph, CG) plus runtime monitors (dynamic behaviours, DB) was tested on an extended blicket task where the rule changes mid-run. CG improved reasoning when reasoning was possible; DB made the agent notice the rule had changed.
numbers: 1,085 trials; Claude Sonnet 4.5 acts, Haiku 4.5 evaluates triggers. Reasoning-eligible accuracy: Base 73.3% (22/30), CG 93.9% (31/33; p=0.038, h=0.59), CG+DB 95.3% (41/43). Raw accuracy, hidden moderator easy: Base 87.3%, CG 77.3%, CG+DB 89.1% (CG vs CG+DB p=0.015 one-tailed). CG accounts for 94% of the reasoning-eligible gain. Exactly-N trap rate CG 28.0% (14/50) vs CG+DB 6.0% (3/50), p=0.003.
limits: Single model family; no scaffold effect in the stochastic condition (76.7% / 76.7% / 73.3%); some one-tailed tests; preprint under review; authors are from a company selling agents.
agent_relevance: Best existing example of a scaffold of our type on a blicket paradigm. Honest note: CG alone lowered raw accuracy because it triggered the rule switch yet did not re-test.

source: Alderete et al. (2026) Dynamic-behaviour monitor DB4: detecting contradiction of an established model
finding: A code-side monitor that fires when an observation contradicts the agent's confirmed model is a necessary condition for revision.
numbers: DB4 sensitivity 100% across five datasets (post-switch correct episodes); positive predictive value 90.5% to 100%. The four PPV failures were downstream reasoning errors.
limits: Sensitivity measured only over post-switch correct episodes; an earlier internal figure of 94.4% used a different denominator (the paper's own footnote).
agent_relevance: Matches G1: doubt only on a signal. A contradiction detector is a better trigger than a schedule.

source: Search note, this session: LLM studies of the Cook et al. ambiguity-gated play paradigm
finding: No paper found that reproduces the Cook, Goodman and Schulz (2011) bead-toy design with an LLM. The nearest are blicket-based active-learning studies (c11-c20), which test how models explore after evidence, not whether play changes between ambiguous and unambiguous evidence.
numbers: Two web searches (children plus ambiguous evidence; blicket plus Little Alchemy) returned the studies above. The search quota then ran out and the arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs returned HTTP 429, so coverage of 2025-2026 preprints is incomplete.
limits: Absence of evidence after limited search; not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: The ambiguity gate for our agent (explore only while two or more hypotheses stay live) has child evidence but no LLM validation. Mark [S] and test it.
